wheelchair.
Discussion: Cocaine-induced spinal cord infarctions are rare, with few
documented cases. The pathogenesis of spinal cord infarct remains
poorly understood, but may include hypertension, vasoconstriction,
thrombosis, and vasospasm. Similarly, prognosis is difﬁcult to assess. In
our case, the patient’s underlying copper and zinc deﬁciencies may
have limited his recovery. Copper and zinc are essential cofactors for
the functioning of superoxide dismutase, an antioxidant with neuro-
protective and neurorestorative properties. Decreased levels of su-
peroxide dismutase are associated with worse outcomes following
stroke.
Conclusions: Copper and zinc deﬁciencies may predispose to spinal
cord infarct and can worsen outcomes following spinal cord injury.
Screening and adequate repletion may facilitate recovery. Malnour-
ished individuals, such as drug users, are at increased risk for these
deﬁciencies. Further studies are required before deﬁnitive recom-
mendations for repletion can be made.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 235
Patterns of Intracranial Hemorrhage Based on
Traumatic Brain Injury Etiology
Saranya P. Balakrishnan, MD (Santa Clara Valley Medical Center,
San Jose, California, United States), Reza Ehsanian, MD, PhD,
Laura Jamison, MD, Samantha Sechrist, Nhung Quach, MD,
James Crew, MD, Linda Isaac, PhD
Disclosures: Saranya Balakrishnan: I Have No Relevant Financial Re-
lationships To Disclose
Objective: To describe the patterns between causes of injury and
intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) in non-contrast head CT reports of pa-
tients with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury (TBI).
Design: Non-contrast head CT reports taken within seven days of TBI
were studied in 712 patients (Mean Age ¼ 32 years, SD+17.5) in the
Northern California TBI Model Systems e Longitudinal Study Center
between 1989-2014.
Setting: Tertiary medical center.
Participants: TBI patients.
Interventions: Not applicable.
Main Outcome Measures: ICH, etiology of TBI.
Results: Out of 712 patients with TBI: 89.61% (n ¼638) had ICH; 9.55%
(n¼68) had no ICH in their CT reports and 0.84% (n ¼6) had missing
reports. The etiology of ICH for TBI patients included: vehicular ac-
cidents (54.86%; n ¼350), falls (17.24%; n ¼110), pedestrians (10.03%;
n¼64), assault (n ¼45; 7.05%), gunshot wound (5.80%; n ¼37), sports
(3.13%; n¼20), and other (1.88%; n ¼12). When considering etiology of
focal cortical parenchymal contusion or hemorrhage the percentage of
frontal hemorrhage is highest when compared to other cortical sites
regardless of etiology (61.82% fall, 53.71% vehicle, 60% assault, 56.76%
gun), except for pedestrians where temporal hemorrhage (48.44%) is
slightly higher than frontal (46.88%). Of the 638 patients with ICH:
subarachnoid hemorrhage was most common (67.87%; n ¼433), fol-
lowed by subdural hemorrhage (45.61%; n ¼291), non-cortical hemor-
rhage (23.67%; n ¼151), intraventricular hemorrhage (25.86%; n ¼165),
punctuate hemorrhage (19.91%; n ¼127), epidural hemorrhage
(14.26%; n ¼91).
Conclusions: Based on this database, frontal and temporal lobes are
the most frequently involved areas for focal cortical parenchymal
contusion or hemorrhage for all TBI etiologies. This may help plan
clinical interventions targeting temporal (memory) and frontal (ex-
ecutive function) deﬁcits. Further research is suggested to understand
the correlation between types and cortical sites of ICH with estab-

lished measures of quality of life, cognitive recovery, and functional
recovery in order to better understand the impact on patient
outcomes.
Level of Evidence: Level III
Poster 236
The Use of a Telepresence Communications Robot by
a Patient with Spinal Cord Injury to Aid in Social
Reintegration and “Virtual Mobility”: A Case Report
Stephen A. Erosa, DO (Monteﬁore Medical Center/Albert Einstein
College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, United States), Michelle Stern, MD
Disclosures: Stephen Erosa: I Have No Relevant Financial Relation-
ships To Disclose
Case/Program Description: Our
 73-year-old patient suffered a C5 Asia
B Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) 3 years ago. Due to his socioeconomic situ-
ation, he is a long term resident in an inpatient rehabilitation unit and
has been unable to acquire a power chair. He cannot tolerate sitting
for more than 1 hour without signiﬁcant discomfort. On the physical
exam, he has diffuse spasticity and multiple ﬂexion contractures. His
active cervical range of motion is 30
/C14 in rotation bilateral and 15 /C14 in
ﬂexion and extension. He can actively ﬂex his right wrist and second
Metacarpophalangeal joint with a strength of 4/5. The robot which
stands about 4 feet tall, controlled via Wi-Fi, consists of a two-way
audio video monitor, microphone, speakers, and a wheeled base. Over
3 1-hour sessions he was taught how to steer the robot using an
adaptive computer interface that translates cervical motion into
cursor movements on a laptop computer. To propel the robot, he ac-
tivates a modiﬁed computer mouse using his residual right hand
function.
Setting: Inpatient Rehabilitation Unit.
Results: Although he requires assistance with set up of the
equipment, he is able to navigate the device around corners and
through doorways, independently. He more frequently socializes
with the other patients and staff. Via the robot, he has attained a
sense of “virtual mobility” and is a ble to voluntarily cruise around
the unit.
Discussion: This is the ﬁrst reported case, to our knowledge, of
an individual with SCI using a telepresence communications
robot. The device can be adapted for those with disabilities and
provide them with the ability to have a presence in distant
environments.
Conclusions: Telecommunications robots have the potential to pro-
vide an adjunctive method of mobility and improve the quality of life
of disabled individuals.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 237
Bilateral Hip Fracture During Hospitalization for
Spasm Exacerbation in an Adult with Stiff Person
Syndrome: A Case Report
Tomasz K. Podobinski, DO (University of TX-UT Houston, Houston,
Texas, United States), Paolo C. Mimbella, MD, Michael J. Irvine, DO,
Monica Verduzco-Gutierrez, MD
Disclosures: Tomasz Podobinski: I Have No Relevant Financial Re-
lationships To Disclose
Case/Program Description: The patient is a 47-year-old woman with
history of breast cancer status post left mastectomy and chemo-
therapy who developed signiﬁcant spasms secondary to stiff person
syndrome. She has been hospitalized multiple times for exacerbations
and is treated with IVIG with good results. She has been discharged
with diazepam, methadone and baclofen on outpatient basis. On her
last hospitalization patient has developed recurrent spasms and severe
hip pain. She subsequently developed bilateral hip fractures and was
treated with total hip arthroplasty.
Setting: Tertiary care hospital.
Results: Four months after the bilateral total hip arthroplasty the

patient maintained signiﬁcant hip pain and spasms despite treatment
with diazepam, methadone and baclofen, which decreased her
participation in therapies.

Discussion: This is the ﬁrst reported case, to our knowledge, of
bilateral hip fractures in a female with stiff person syndrome related
spasms despite generally accepted therapy.
Conclusions: Even with widely accepted therapy with diazepam and
baclofen in patients with stiff person syndrome, refractory spasms
may contribute to signiﬁcant forces exerted on bony elements leading
to fractures.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 238
Tumefactive Demyelinating Lesions: Rehabilitation of
a Rare, Debilitating Form of Multiple Sclerosis: A
Case Report
Carrie M. Gould, MD (Marianjoy Rehab Hospital, Wheaton, IL, United
States), Anjum Sayyad, MD, Grace L. Maloney, MD
Disclosures: Carrie Gould: I Have No Relevant Financial Relationships
To Disclose
Case/Program Description: Thirty-year-old woman with multiple
sclerosis presented to academic center with memory loss, ﬂat affect,
anorexia and somnolence of three months’ duration, and with acute
onset confusion, aphasia and MMSE of 14/30. MRI of the brain revealed
subcortical and cortical hyperdense lesions inconsistent with multiple
sclerosis. Brain biopsy was performed noting diffuse demyelinating
process consistent with tumefactive multiple sclerosis. Patient un-
derwent plasmapheresis, Rituximab infusion, and steroid treatment.
Setting: Acute inpatient rehabilitation.
Results: Patient was severely aphasic and confused with marked
auditory and verbal expression deﬁcits and the ability to perform only
one-step tasks inconsistently with simple cues. She communicated
with spontaneous verbal utterances of rote phrases with no contextual
meaning. She was impulsive, requiring an enclosure bed for safety.
Depakote and Inderal were used for agitation and impulsivity. Given
her low attention and concentration, she was started on Ritalin, which
may have precipitated hypersexual behaviors.
Discussion: Tumefactive multiple sclerosis represents an estimated 1
to 2 of 1000 cases of multiple sclerosis with a higher prevalence in
females and a median age of onset of 37 years. Tumefactive multiple
sclerosis is an acute tumor-like variant wherein patients present with
acute large solitary or multiple lesions, often appearing on radiologic
studies as intracranial tumors or gliomas, with mass effect, edema and
enhancement, features that result in inappropriate diagnosis after
unnecessary surgical resection or from biopsy, when many cases are
responsive to glucocorticoid therapy.
Conclusions: Rehabilitation of tumefactive multiple sclerosis is
particularly challenging, given the lack of research and variability in
presentation (usually polysymptomatic, often with confusion, hemi-
paresis or neglect). To our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst reported case in
rehabilitation literature, and physiatrists would beneﬁt from an
awareness of this rare type of multiple sclerosis and the particular
challenges it presents due to its marked morbidity and difﬁculty/
varied response to treatment with glucocorticoids.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 239
Cannabidiol as Treatment for Spasticity: A
Case Report
Amanda K. Morrow, MD (Sinai Hospital of Baltimore/University of
Maryland, Baltimore, Maryland, United States), Henry S. York, MD
Disclosures: Amanda Morrow: I Have No Relevant Financial Relation-
ships To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 27-year-old man with C7 American
Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS) B spinal cord injury
from a remote diving accident complicated by severe spasticity

requiring intrathecal baclofen (ITB) therapy presented to clinic for
follow-up. His ITB pump was due for replacement so he elected to self-
medicate with an over-the-counter (OTC) orally-ingested cannabinoid
oil that contains high cannabidiol (CBD) and minimal delta-9-tetrahy-
drocannabinol (THC). His starting dose of CBD was 12.5 micrograms
(mcg) twice daily while his ITB dose was 507.3 micrograms per day
(mcg/d). One month later, he increased his CBD dose to 25 mcg twice
daily and requested that his pump dosage be decreased to 420.0 mcg/
d. Over the following two months, his pump dosage was decreased
further to 324.4 mcg/d.
Setting: Outpatient clinic.
Results: He tolerated a reduction of 183 micrograms (36.1%) of
intrathecal baclofen while using CBD over 3 months. He reported
excellent spasticity relief; however, his most recent examination
found considerable spasticity and clonus throughout his lower limbs.
Functionally, he was able to maintain full-time employment and safely
parent his 1-year-old child. He denied any adverse side effects from
CBD including cognitive changes. He continues to use CBD to in order
to avoid pump replacement.
Discussion: CBD, the primary non-psychoactive cannabinoid in
cannabis has been recently studied in an open-label, uncontrolled
interventional trial for treatment-resistant epilepsy. Though cannabi-
noids have previously been reported to reduce spasticity, this is the
ﬁrst reported case of possible dose equivalence of CBD with 183 mi-
crograms of intrathecal baclofen. The patient’s signiﬁcant spasticity
on physical exam may suggest a placebo response, which has been
widely described with many cannabis-derived treatments. Concerns
remain regarding the purity of OTC cannabidiol preparations and acute
and long-term neurologic toxicity.
Conclusions: Further research is needed to understand the safety and
efﬁcacy of cannabidiol as a treatment for spasticity.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 240
Importance of Recognizing Sinking Skin Flap
Syndrome/Syndrome of Trephine: A Case Report
Kristen M. Brusky, DO (University of Rochester, Rochester, New York,
United States), Franchesca Konig Toro, MD, Nicole A. Strong, DO,
Nathan Odom, MD
Disclosures: Kristen Brusky: I Have No Relevant Financial Relation-
ships To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 66-year-old man presented to the
emergency department in critical condition with a Glasgow Coma
score of 3 following a 10-foot fall onto concrete. He was diagnosed
with bilateral subdural hematomas, urgently intubated, and taken to
the operating room for a right hemicraniectomy with external ven-
tricular drain placement. On post-operative day 21, the patient was
transferred to acute rehabilitation for neurological stimulation trial
due to a Rancho Los Amigos Level of 4. On rehabilitation day 5, he
developed worsening mental status and left arm weakness. The
following morning, his left arm was ﬂaccid. Subsequent head CT
demonstrated 9 mm right to left midline shift with paradoxical uncal
and subfalcine herniation. The patient was transferred out of the
rehabilitation unit acutely for consideration of cranioplasty.
Setting: Inpatient rehabilitation unit at a tertiary care hospital.
Results: The patient’s initial work up, including spot electroenceph-
alogram, was without abnormality. He was diagnosed with Sinking Skin
Flap Syndrome (SSFS) and underwent cranioplasty within 48 hours of
transfer. Strength dramatically improved and he was admitted back to

acute rehabilitation on post-operative day 4. He required minimal
assistance
for ambulation and was discharged home within 2 weeks at
a modiﬁed independent level with a single post cane.
Discussion: SSFS is an unusual neurological syndrome, which occurs
following removal of a large cranial bone ﬂap. Its presentation can
mimic stroke, subclinical seizures, metabolic derangement or infec-
tion. The true incidence of SSFS is unknown, but is expected to in-
crease given the rise in decompressive craniectomies.
